title: Ola Electric Q2 Loss Down 13% To ₹362 Cr, Revenue Dips 39%
summary: Ola Electric Q2 revenue dips 39 percent while consolidated net loss narrows 13 percent
detailed: Ola Electric reported a 13% year-over-year decline in net loss to ₹362 Cr for Q2 FY27, while operating revenue dropped 39% to ₹421 Cr.
The EV maker's total income fell 41% to ₹448 Cr and total expenses declined 28% to ₹639 Cr compared to the same period last year.
The company is transitioning from a direct-to-consumer model to a dealer-led network, onboarding 255 dealer partners and opening over 300 stores by November 8.
Ola Electric stated that demand is no longer its primary constraint, with the main bottleneck now being the pace at which its supply chain can scale production.
sentences: However, the E2W maker’s top line continued to face pressure on its top line, with operating revenue declining 39% YoY to ₹421 Cr from ₹690 Cr.
On a sequential basis, the company’s loss widened 8% from ₹336 Cr in Q1 FY27, while revenue declined 7% from ₹455 Cr.
Including other income of ₹27 Cr, Ola Electric’s total income stood at ₹448 Cr, down 41% YoY from ₹756 Cr.
Total expenses declined 28% YoY to ₹639 Cr from ₹893 Cr, although they rose 3% QoQ.
Ola Electric’s operating EBITDA loss increased 7% YoY to ₹218 Cr.
Gross margin stood at 29.9%, against 30.5% in Q1 FY27 and 30.9% in the year-ago quarter.
Ola Electric attributed the sequential moderation largely to higher commodity costs, partly offset by price increases.
The automotive business contributed ₹420 Cr to revenue, while the cell business generated ₹3 Cr.
Inter-segment revenue, representing cells used in Ola’s own vehicles, stood at ₹2 Cr.
The automotive business reported an operating EBITDA loss of ₹120 Cr, 2.6 times the loss in the year-ago quarter.
The cell business, meanwhile, narrowed its operating EBITDA loss by 36% YoY to ₹32 Cr.
Against this backdrop, Ola Electric is attempting to reset its distribution and cost structure, while ramping up in-house cell manufacturing.
The company’s immediate focus is on improving vehicle availability, reducing operating expenses and easing working capital requirements.
A key part of this reset is Ola Electric’s transition from its erstwhile touted D2C distribution model to a more streamlined dealer-led network.
It had announced this shift earlier in Q2 (in August) and subsequently opened dealer stores on September 4.
As of November 8, it had onboarded 255 dealer partners and established more than 300 stores.
It now has set a target of operating 450 stores by December and 700 by March 2027.
Ola Electric stopped accepting orders through its D2C stores from November 1.
Most company-owned stores are expected to close by December, with all new vehicle production routed to the dealer network.
The transition is expected to change the company’s cost structure.

Dealers purchase vehicles from Ola Electric and maintain inventory at their own outlets, reducing the company’s need to manage a self-owned retail network as well as finance the inventory held at its stores.
As a result, the EV maker expects operating expenses to come down by ₹50 Cr.
In its shareholder letter, it said operating expenses stood at ₹369 Cr in Q2 FY27, against ₹390 Cr in Q1, excluding a one-time non-cash reversal of ₹57 Cr in the June quarter.
However, the transition could weigh on gross margins in the near term.
This pressure comes at the behest of the pay it dolls out as commissions to its dealers.
The cost structure here is yet to be revealed.
Ola Electric expects the dealer commission structure to moderate over the next two to three quarters as the network stabilises.
It expects the shift to start improving operating margins from Q3 FY27 onwards.
“Gross margins will come down a bit, but operating margins will meaningfully improve,” founder and Chairman Bhavish Aggarwal said during the earnings call.
The company said dealer sell-through was improving, with channel inventory at around 15 days.
It also reported that dealers had begun placing repeat orders, indicating improving movement through the new distribution network.
In its shareholder letter, Ola Electric said demand was no longer its primary constraint.
It pointed instead to the pace at which its supply chain could scale production to meet demand.
“We reset our business and rebuilt it on a more sustainable model, which we are now growing.
The main headline of Q2 FY27 is that demand is no longer our constraint; supply is.
The constraint is not our manufacturing capacity but our supply chain’s ramp-up, which we are scaling rapidly,” it noted.
Production has remained broadly flat for several months but has started increasing month-on-month.
Ola Electric expects to produce around 25,000 vehicles in December.
The company expects further cost savings from integrating its in-house lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells and Gen 4 platform into its vehicles from Q4 FY27 onwards.
Ola Electric continues to operate with negative cash flows.
Its consolidated operating cash flow stood at negative ₹188 Cr, while free cash flow was negative ₹371 Cr during the quarter.
However, Aggarwal believes that operating cash flows were stabilising and improving sequentially.
He attributed much of the difference between operating and free cash flow to capital expenditure at the Gigafactory.
The company said that it has strengthened its balance sheet through the recent qualified institutional placement (QIP) and rights issue over the past few months.
The company raised ₹780 Cr via its QIP in June and another ₹1,000 Cr via a rights issue that culminated last week.
Total borrowings declined to ₹1,819 Cr in September 2026 from ₹3,132 Cr in December 2024.
Auto borrowings fell more sharply to ₹337 Cr from ₹2,422 Cr during the same period.

“With low auto debt, a healthy gross margin and cost structure, and a much improved working capital cycle under the dealer model, we expect auto to generate free cash flow in the near term,” the company said.
Further, the dealer-led model can also improve working capital because dealers pay for vehicles when placing orders and hold inventory at their own stores.
This reduces the amount of working capital Ola Electric needs to deploy across its distribution network.
The company also expects changes to the GST refund mechanism, effective November 1, 2026, to ease working capital requirements.
Under the revised framework, refunds under the inverted duty structure will cover GST paid on services in addition to raw materials.
A provision for 90% auto-approval of eligible refunds is also expected to reduce the refund cycle from three to four months to one to two months.
Aggarwal said Ola Electric had already started reducing its GST receivables through internal operational improvements over the preceding two quarters.
Of the roughly ₹1,000 Cr in GST receivables discussed during the earnings call, management estimated that 30-40% was linked to the inverted duty structure.
The remaining amount would largely be adjusted against future business and should not be treated as immediately realisable cash.
Beyond its automotive business, Ola Electric is looking to improve the economics of its cell manufacturing operations, which it sees as a key growth engine.
The company claims to have achieved the scheduled commercial operation date (SCOD) for its 6 GWh cell manufacturing capacity ahead of schedule.
It is now focused on improving production yields and scaling output at the Gigafactory.
NMC cell yields were already in the mid-70% range, and the company expects them to reach 80-85% over the next few months before progressing towards 90%.
